title: Preparing For AI-Driven Chip Design And Verification
gist: A panel of EDA/chip-design AI executives (ChipAgents, Silvaco, Moores Lab AI, Breker, Verific, Silimate) argues agentic AI is dissolving traditional design/verification job boundaries while remaining an unexplainable black box that requires sandboxing and independent benchmarks, and debates whether AI-driven design efficiency will erode Nvidia's fab-capacity-driven margins or simply reward chipmakers further, even as software-layer EDA startups are suddenly raising capital far more easily than hardware ever could.

insights.claim: Generative AI can produce millions of design options almost instantly, which shifts the critical bottleneck in chip engineering from generating options to human judgment about which options matter, pushing that judgment role up to architects and supervisors who direct multiple AI agents.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: EDA/AI vendors that build strong human-in-the-loop curation and supervisory tooling (not just generation) will capture more value than pure generation tools as option volume stops being the constraint.
insights.quote: you can generate different options — millions of options very quickly. So human judgment of which options really matter becomes very critical.
insights.locator: SE: How will AI affect engineering jobs?

insights.claim: Traditional functional silos in chip development — design engineering, verification, layout, and package design — are breaking down as AI enables end-to-end workflows, forcing every engineer to rapidly learn adjacent domains and direct AI agents across the full design cycle.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Watch for EDA vendors and chip design teams reorganizing around cross-functional 'AI-directing' engineer roles rather than discipline-specific specialists.
insights.locator: If we look at the industry right now, we still have a definition like a design engineering group

insights.claim: The cost-per-transistor learning curve is a durable, decades-long economic truism (comparable to century-long cost-per-pound curves in commodities like copper) that AI disruption does not break in the long run, even though China's proposed reframing to 'cost per computation' is a different way of measuring the same underlying trend.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Investors should treat AI-driven chip design gains as accelerating the existing cost-decline curve rather than creating a structurally new economic regime — pricing power still erodes over time regardless of the metric used.
insights.quote: It comes down for lots of reasons, like depreciation and experience. And anything that is measurable as an equivalent unit of capability will always be on a learning curve.
insights.locator: SE: Is the learning curve changing with AI?

insights.claim: New engineering graduates may not need to understand AI's internal workings to trust and productively use agentic design tools, similar to how synthesis-tool adoption didn't require deep understanding from newer engineers, while veteran engineers who insist on explainability risk being displaced.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Talent and hiring strategy in chip design should anticipate a generational split: newer engineers trained to operate AI tools on faith may out-compete veterans who demand full transparency before adoption.
insights.quote: maybe there is hope for the new grads, and maybe the older guys will get kicked out.
insights.locator: Experienced engineers need to understand what the heck is going on to trust it

themes.theme: AI as an unexplainable black box in verification

insights.claim: Even after digging into embeddings, matrix multiplication, and training mechanics, a chip-design AI executive concluded neural networks' ability to generalize to unseen data (e.g., correctly classifying a never-before-seen dog/cat image) cannot be logically explained, and believes it may never be fully understood.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Teams deploying agentic AI in chip design/verification should plan for permanent, irreducible black-box risk rather than expecting future interpretability research to close the gap.
insights.quote: I believe we will never know.
insights.locator: How do we add visibility into AI?

insights.claim: The biggest danger from AI in chip design isn't obviously wrong output — it's incorrect output that looks correct, which is very hard for a human reviewer to catch, making independently constructed benchmark datasets (distinct from training data) essential for verifying agentic AI solutions.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Due diligence on AI-driven EDA vendors should specifically probe whether their verification benchmarks are held out from training data, not just whether accuracy metrics look strong.
insights.quote: The biggest risk is not that AI generates something wrong. It’s that it generates something wrong that looks correct.
insights.locator: The biggest risk is not that AI generates something wrong

insights.claim: Reliability of an agentic AI design tool should be established empirically over time — through thousands of daily users successfully taping out real chips with it — rather than assumed or proven at launch, since a vendor with a large real-world usage base has a genuine trust signal newer entrants lack.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Evaluate agentic EDA tools by production tape-out track record and daily active real-design usage, not by vendor claims or synthetic demos.
insights.quote: if the tool has been used by thousands of users every day on their real design and succesfully taped out, you can keep evolving from there
insights.locator: A common question from the customer side

themes.theme: Agent safety, sandboxing, and corruption risk

insights.claim: Because engineers cannot know in advance whether an AI agent has been corrupted or compromised, safe deployment requires preventive sandboxing — containerizing agents, restricting their permissions so they can't act outside scope — plus auditability and checkpointed state so a corrupted or failed run can be traced and rolled back.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Any agentic chip-design pipeline should be assessed on concrete safety infrastructure (containerization, permission scoping, audit logs, checkpoint/recovery) rather than vendor assurances about model quality.
insights.quote: The smartest thing would be to sandbox it. Put some kind of container around it, put in some permissions so that it can’t reach outside of its scope.
insights.locator: How do you know the agents haven’t been corrupted

insights.claim: AI agents developing token-optimized 'secret languages' between themselves (as Anthropic has reported) is not an intentional obfuscation behavior but an emergent optimization for communication cost, and can be prevented by explicit up-front instructions forcing agents to use human-readable formats like JSON.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: System designers building multi-agent chip-design pipelines should hard-code human-readable communication schemas as a guardrail against invisible inter-agent behavior, rather than treating it as an unsolvable emergent risk.
insights.quote: Anthropic mentioned something about secret languages agents developed. I don’t think that’s something they’re built to do.
insights.locator: Anthropic mentioned something about secret languages agents developed

themes.theme: Who captures the economic value of AI-driven design

insights.claim: EDA companies have historically captured only a fixed ~14% R&D-budget-linked share of semiconductor industry revenue over the past 30-40 years, missing the outsized rewards captured by chipmakers like Nvidia, which became a multi-trillion-dollar company by selling more chips at higher prices and being directly rewarded for design productivity gains.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Structural EDA revenue-share economics (percent of R&D budget) cap upside even if AI massively boosts EDA tool productivity — investors should distinguish EDA vendors trying to break this ceiling from those staying within it.
insights.quote: The R&D for the semiconductor industry is about 14% over the last 30 or 40 years, and it grows along with the revenue of the semiconductor companies.
insights.locator: Historically, EDA, for the majority of its market

insights.claim: Silvaco's CEO wants to expand EDA revenue capture beyond the traditional R&D-budget percentage by going after the semiconductor manufacturing budget instead, seeking new revenue models where EDA vendors are paid more than a fixed slice of R&D spend.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Track EDA vendors pivoting pricing/product strategy toward manufacturing or yield budgets as a signal of attempts to break out of the low-growth R&D-percentage revenue ceiling.
insights.quote: In my own case, I want to go after the manufacturing budget. That’s a great one.
insights.locator: What you’d really like to see is for that to change

insights.claim: If AI makes chip design dramatically cheaper, it could increase competition against dominant players like Nvidia and compress their profit margins, since cheaper design enabled by the EDA industry and the underlying cost-per-transistor learning curve lowers barriers to entry for challengers.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A sustained drop in chip-design cost via AI/EDA tooling is a bearish signal for incumbent GPU/accelerator margin durability and a bullish signal for new entrants targeting Nvidia's workloads.
insights.quote: if you make the chip-building so much cheaper, that will create more competition for people like Nvidia, and they won’t be able to get that much profit margin anymore
insights.locator: I agree with you. But on the other hand

insights.claim: AMD is cited as a real, strengthening competitor to Nvidia after years of failed attempts by others to compete, suggesting the more durable path to challenging Nvidia is producing genuinely more innovative chips (potentially AI-assisted) rather than just cheaper ones.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: AMD's competitive traction against Nvidia is framed by an industry insider as a live, ongoing shift worth monitoring alongside AI-enabled design innovation as the real differentiator, not price alone.
insights.quote: People are trying to compete with Nvidia, and they’ve failed. Maybe they’re starting to get there now. AMD is getting stronger.
insights.locator: Is it cheaper or more innovative?

insights.claim: Because custom chip designs for specific algorithms now cost roughly $200 million each and that spend can't scale indefinitely, the next architectural shift will be toward 'morphable chips' that can reconfigure their connectivity, memory partitioning, and instruction sets on the fly to handle different algorithms at different times.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Watch for reconfigurable/morphable chip architectures as a hedge against unsustainable per-design NRE costs — a potential investment theme distinct from both fixed ASICs and general-purpose GPUs.
insights.quote: You’ll see chips that can reconfigure themselves in connectivity, memory partitioning, instruction sets, and be able to switch during processing to do different algorithms at different times.
insights.locator: you can’t just continue to spend $200 million per chip design

insights.claim: AI-driven chip-design startups are targeting semiconductor companies' large and growing AI budgets — a separate, expanding pool distinct from the fixed, slow-growing traditional EDA budget — with trillion-dollar customers like Micron, Marvell, and Nvidia already spending in this new category.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: The addressable market for AI-native chip-design tooling should be sized against corporate AI budgets, not legacy EDA spend, implying a materially larger TAM than traditional EDA market-share analysis suggests.
insights.quote: It’s a huge and growing potential market. The existing EDA market is stable, and the budget is fixed, and growth will be limited.
insights.locator: Regarding competition and who will eventually make more money

insights.claim: Nvidia's outsized profit margins have been partly driven by TSMC's cautious, slow ramp of AI-related fab capacity because TSMC was initially unsure the AI demand was durable, creating an artificial supply constraint; as fab capacity expands and specialized-chip cadence increases, the resulting larger addressable market could let more players profit along the same growth trajectory.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Fab capacity expansion is a concrete catalyst to watch for margin compression at scarcity-driven leaders like Nvidia and margin expansion opportunities for a broader set of specialized-chip players.
insights.quote: TSMC took their time in ramping up capacity for the AI market because they weren’t sure whether or not it was going to be a real thing.
insights.locator: One of the reasons for Nvidia’s insane profit margin

themes.theme: VC funding shift toward AI-native EDA startups

insights.claim: Software-layer AI-driven EDA startups like Silimate can land their first annual license contract within a year of founding, making them dramatically more fundable than traditional hardware startups that require years and $100 million-plus funding tranches just to reach a minimally functional first test chip.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Investors comparing hardware-adjacent AI startups should weight time-to-revenue heavily: software-layer chip-design tooling can de-risk capital far faster than silicon-first hardware bets.
insights.quote: We got our first annual license contract in less than a year from when we started.
insights.locator: One of the hard things about raising capital for a hardware startup

insights.claim: Silvaco's CEO spent five years unsuccessfully chasing VC funding for a prior hardware venture (Cornami), with investors dismissing hardware pitches outright, illustrating how dramatically VC appetite for chip-related startups has shifted since Nvidia's rise made huge valuations possible before proven products.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: The current willingness of VCs to fund pre-product semiconductor/AI-chip startups at rich valuations is a recent regime change, not the historical norm — a reversal that could unwind if AI-chip sentiment cools.
insights.quote: I spent five years chasing VCs for Cornami.
insights.locator: The VCs were spoiled by the software industry

insights.claim: Major semiconductor incumbents — TSMC, Micron, and Ericsson — are directly investing in AI-driven chip-design startups, treating the current moment as a critical inflection point that is reshaping the future of chip design and enabling faster fundraising for the sector.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Track strategic (not just financial) investment from TSMC, Micron, and Ericsson into AI-EDA startups as a leading indicator of which agentic design tools gain incumbent validation and distribution.
insights.quote: This is the right inflection point for the entire industry. A lot of investments are coming from the semiconductor companies, led by TSMC, Micron, and Ericsson.
insights.locator: This is the right inflection point for the entire industry
